title: What replaced ZooKeeper in Kafka 4.0 (KRaft), and why does it matter?
shortTitle: What replaced ZooKeeper in Kafka 4.0 (KRaft) and why it matters

s1_definition.profdef: In Kafka 4.0, Apache ZooKeeper was fully removed and replaced by KRaft, which stands for Kafka Raft metadata mode. KRaft moves all cluster metadata — topics, partitions, replica assignments, configurations, and access control lists — into an internal Kafka metadata topic managed by a quorum of controller nodes using the Raft consensus protocol. This eliminates the separate ZooKeeper ensemble that Kafka historically depended on, giving Kafka a single, self-managed system for both data and metadata with faster metadata operations, simpler operations, and better scalability.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India used to rely on a separate outside agency (ZooKeeper) to keep the master list of which vault holds which ledger, who is in charge, and the rules. Every time something changed, the bank had to phone that outside agency, which was slow and was one more thing that could fail. KRaft is like the bank bringing that master list in-house and letting its own senior managers (controller nodes) agree on it among themselves using a clear voting rule (Raft). Now there is one organization to run, decisions are faster, and there is no outside dependency to break.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka 4.0 replaced ZooKeeper with KRaft, storing cluster metadata inside Kafka itself via Raft consensus, making Kafka simpler, faster, and more scalable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Kafka 4.0, Apache ZooKeeper was fully removed and replaced by KRaft, which stands for Kafka Raft metadata mode. KRaft moves all cluster metadata — topics, partitions, replica assignments, configurations, and access control lists — into an internal Kafka metadata topic managed by a quorum of controller nodes using the Raft consensus protocol. This eliminates the separate ZooKeeper ensemble that Kafka historically depended on, giving Kafka a single, self-managed system for both data and metadata with faster metadata operations, simpler operations, and better scalability.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India used to rely on a separate outside agency (ZooKeeper) to keep the master list of which vault holds which ledger, who is in charge, and the rules. Every time something changed, the bank had to phone that outside agency, which was slow and was one more thing that could fail. KRaft is like the bank bringing that master list in-house and letting its own senior managers (controller nodes) agree on it among themselves using a clear voting rule (Raft). Now there is one organization to run, decisions are faster, and there is no outside dependency to break.

**One line to remember:** Kafka 4.0 replaced ZooKeeper with KRaft, storing cluster metadata inside Kafka itself via Raft consensus, making Kafka simpler, faster, and more scalable.

sections.s2_technical:
For most of its history, Kafka used ZooKeeper as an external coordination service to store cluster metadata: the list of brokers, topic and partition definitions, which broker leads each partition, configurations, and ACLs. Brokers watched ZooKeeper for changes, and a single broker acted as the controller that pushed metadata updates. This worked but had real drawbacks — you had to deploy, secure, tune, and monitor a second distributed system, and ZooKeeper became a scalability bottleneck as the number of partitions grew into the hundreds of thousands.

KRaft removes ZooKeeper entirely. Metadata now lives in an internal, replicated Kafka log topic named `__cluster_metadata`, and a dedicated set of controller nodes forms a Raft quorum to manage it. Raft is a consensus algorithm in which the quorum elects a leader (the active controller) and replicates an ordered log of metadata changes to the follower controllers. A metadata change is committed once a majority of the controllers have it, which is the same durability idea Kafka already uses for data, now applied to metadata.

Because metadata is itself an event log, brokers consume metadata changes the same way consumers read a topic — they follow the metadata log and apply updates incrementally. This is far more efficient than the old model of watching ZooKeeper and reloading large snapshots. The result is that leader elections and metadata propagation are much faster, and the cluster can support vastly more partitions without the old ZooKeeper ceiling.

Operationally, KRaft simplifies everything. There is one system to install, secure, upgrade, and monitor instead of two. You can run controllers as separate dedicated nodes for larger clusters, or in combined mode where a node is both a broker and a controller for smaller deployments. Configuration uses a single process role setting, `process.roles=broker,controller` or just one of them, and a quorum voter list. Startup uses a formatted cluster id rather than ZooKeeper connection strings.

Why it matters is a combination of performance, simplicity, and reliability. Faster controller failover means shorter unavailability windows during a controller crash, which for a bank means less disruption. Supporting millions of partitions means Kafka scales to very large event-driven architectures. Removing the external dependency shrinks the attack surface and the number of failure modes, and it removes the operational burden of keeping ZooKeeper healthy, patched, and in sync. It also unifies security and configuration under one system.

The senior-level nuance is the migration and version context. KRaft became production-ready in Kafka 3.3, ZooKeeper was deprecated through the 3.x line, and Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper support completely, so new 4.0 clusters are KRaft-only. Teams upgrading from older ZooKeeper-based clusters must perform a migration to KRaft before moving to 4.0. In practice this means planning the controller quorum sizing — typically three or five controllers for an odd-numbered majority — ensuring the metadata log is on reliable storage, and validating the migration in staging. The durability and fault-tolerance principles of the controller quorum mirror those of data replication: a quorum of three controllers tolerates one failure, a quorum of five tolerates two.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is upgrading its Kafka platform to 4.0 and must move from ZooKeeper to KRaft, and the platform team models how metadata management changes.

Problem 1 — The old cluster depended on a separate ZooKeeper ensemble that the team had to patch and monitor, and it was becoming a bottleneck as partition counts grew. This is exactly what KRaft removes by bringing metadata inside Kafka.

Problem 2 — When the controller failed, metadata recovery through ZooKeeper was slow, causing longer unavailability for transfer topics. This is exactly what KRaft improves with fast Raft-based controller failover from the metadata quorum.

Problem 3 — The team must size the controller quorum so the cluster tolerates a controller failure without losing the metadata that tells it which broker leads each partition. This is exactly the Raft majority rule — a quorum of three tolerates one failure.

The mini-project simulates metadata management before and after. We build a `MetadataChange` domain object, a `ZookeeperMetadataStore` representing the old external approach, a `KRaftControllerQuorum` that replicates metadata changes to a quorum and commits on majority with fast leader election, and a `MetadataService` that applies a change and reports availability. The demo applies a topic-creation metadata change under KRaft, then fails the active controller to show fast failover and continued metadata operations.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the demo
javac com/bank/kraft/demo/KRaftDemo.java
java com.bank.kraft.demo.KRaftDemo

# Format and start a KRaft cluster (Kafka 4.0, no ZooKeeper)
KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID=$(kafka-storage.sh random-uuid)
kafka-storage.sh format -t $KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID -c config/kraft/server.properties
kafka-server-start.sh config/kraft/server.properties
# server.properties: process.roles=broker,controller ; controller.quorum.voters=1@c1:9093,2@c2:9093,3@c3:9093
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is several metadata changes: a topic creation and two leader elections, applied under the old ZooKeeper store and the new KRaft quorum.

Step 1 — For contrast, the legacy ZooKeeper store applies a create-topic change through its external ensemble. The log notes this is slower and requires operating a separate system.

Step 2 — The KRaft controller quorum is created with three controllers c1, c2, c3, and c1 is the active controller. The majority needed is two.

Step 3 — The create-topic metadata change for transfers is applied. The quorum replicates it to the controllers, and because all three copy it, that is at least the majority of two, so the change is committed to the internal __cluster_metadata log. The metadata is now available through the active controller c1.

Step 4 — A leader-election metadata change for transfers-P0 is applied the same way and committed by majority, showing routine metadata operations flowing through the quorum as an ordered log.

Step 5 — The active controller c1 crashes. The quorum removes it and performs a fast Raft re-election, promoting c2 as the new active controller. Because the metadata log was already replicated to the majority, no metadata is lost. A new leader-election change for transfers-P1 is then applied and committed by the surviving quorum, proving that metadata operations continue seamlessly after a controller failure — the key improvement over the slower ZooKeeper-based recovery.

```

  ── State Diagram: a controller ───────────────────────────────

  [FOLLOWER] → wins Raft election → [ACTIVE CONTROLLER]
  [ACTIVE] → crashes → survivors → fast election → new [ACTIVE]
  commit requires MAJORITY of controllers alive

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. meta.applyChange(CREATE_TOPIC) → quorum.replicate() → majority → commit
  2. meta.applyChange(ELECT_LEADER P0) → commit
  3. quorum.failController("c1") → fast re-election → c2 active
  4. meta.applyChange(ELECT_LEADER P1) → committed by survivors

  Contract for replicate(change):
    Pre:  a majority of controllers alive
    Post: change appended to metadata log and visible to brokers
    Rule: no quorum → reject; majority → commit (like data durability)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In Kafka 4.0, ZooKeeper was completely removed and replaced by KRaft, which stands for Kafka Raft metadata mode. Historically Kafka used ZooKeeper as a separate external service to store all cluster metadata — brokers, topics, partitions, which broker leads each partition, configurations, and ACLs. KRaft moves all of that metadata into an internal replicated Kafka log called the cluster metadata topic, managed by a dedicated quorum of controller nodes using the Raft consensus protocol.

The way it works is that the controllers form a Raft quorum, elect an active controller, and replicate an ordered log of metadata changes. A change is committed once a majority of controllers have it, exactly like Kafka's data durability but applied to metadata. Brokers then follow this metadata log and apply changes incrementally, which is far more efficient than the old model of watching ZooKeeper and reloading snapshots.

Why it matters comes down to performance, simplicity, and reliability. Controller failover is much faster because a new active controller is elected from the quorum and the metadata log is already replicated, so for a bank that means shorter unavailability windows during a controller crash. KRaft scales to millions of partitions, removing the old ZooKeeper bottleneck. And operationally there is now one system to install, secure, upgrade, and monitor instead of two, which shrinks both the attack surface and the number of failure modes.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, moving to KRaft means metadata operations like topic creation and leader election flow through the controller quorum and survive a controller failure with a fast re-election and no metadata loss, which previously was a slower and riskier recovery through ZooKeeper. The senior point I always add is the version context and migration: KRaft became production-ready in Kafka 3.3, was the recommended mode through 3.x, and 4.0 is KRaft-only, so upgrading from an older ZooKeeper cluster requires a planned migration. I size the controller quorum as an odd number, typically three or five, so a quorum of three tolerates one controller failure and five tolerates two, mirroring the same majority-based fault tolerance Kafka already uses for data.
